sources.title: International guidelines for groin hernia management
Guidelines for emergency repair of complicated abdominal wall hernias

indications: Any irreducible, incarcerated or strangulated hernia, as an emergency.
A femoral hernia should be repaired promptly whether or not it is symptomatic, because the strangulation risk is high.
Watchful waiting is reasonable for a minimally symptomatic reducible inguinal hernia in a man, and is a discussion rather than a default.
contraindications: Active infection at the operative site: mesh is avoided in a contaminated field.
A patient who cannot tolerate the anaesthetic required. Local anaesthesia is often the answer rather than deferral.
Untreated ascites, prostatism or chronic cough will cause recurrence if not addressed first.
preparation: Examine standing and lying, both groins, and document reducibility and the cough impulse.
Optimise the driver: constipation, cough, prostatism, weight.
Antibiotic prophylaxis according to local policy for mesh implantation.
Consent must include chronic groin pain, recurrence, injury to cord structures and testicular atrophy, urinary retention and seroma.
positioning: Supine, slight Trendelenburg to reduce the hernia contents and empty the veins.
Bladder emptied before the patient comes to theatre.
Arm out on the side of the anaesthetist; the operating side kept clear.
equipment: Standard general set, self-retaining retractor, a fine dissecting set.
Flat polypropylene mesh of adequate size, and non-absorbable or slowly absorbable suture for fixation.
Local anaesthetic for field block and for post-operative comfort even under general anaesthesia.
anatomy: The inguinal canal runs from the deep ring, an opening in the transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, to the superficial ring in the external oblique aponeurosis.
An indirect hernia passes through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, within the cord. A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle, medial to them.
A femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, and is the one that strangulates.
The cord contains the vas deferens, the testicular and cremasteric vessels, the pampiniform plexus, and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
Three nerves are at risk and should be identified and preserved or deliberately divided: the ilioinguinal, the iliohypogastric and the genital branch of the genitofemoral.
criticalSafety: Identify the three nerves before placing mesh. Chronic groin pain is the commonest long-term complication of this operation and it starts here.
Always inspect the femoral canal, particularly in women and in any obstructed presentation.
In a strangulated hernia, do not reduce non-viable bowel into the abdomen. Get control of the sac before you reduce.
structuresAtRisk: Femoral vein, when suturing medially and inferiorly
Bladder, in a large direct or sliding hernia
commonErrors: Missing a coexisting femoral hernia because only the inguinal one was looked for.
Mesh that is too small, or not fixed adequately to the pubic tubercle: the medial corner is where recurrence happens.
Mesh placed under tension or without a slit accommodating the cord, causing pain and recurrence.
Forcible reduction of a tender hernia, reducing dead bowel en masse into the abdomen.
complications: Chronic post-operative inguinal pain, in a meaningful minority of patients.
Recurrence, most often at the pubic tubercle.
Seroma or haematoma; scrotal haematoma after a large indirect sac.
Urinary retention, especially in older men after spinal anaesthesia.
Mesh infection, which is uncommon but may require mesh removal.
postop: Day-case surgery for most patients, with simple analgesia and early return to normal activity.
No lifting restriction beyond comfort in a tension-free repair; advise activity as tolerated.
Warn about scrotal swelling and bruising, which is common and alarming to the patient.
Review any new severe or burning groin pain: early recognition of chronic pain gives more options.

steps.emphasis: Mark the correct side with the patient standing, with the hernia visible.
A sac is usually not sent. Any resected bowel or an unexpected mass always is.

step.hern.incision.title: Incision and opening the inguinal canal
step.hern.incision.why: A correctly placed incision gives access to both rings and to the femoral canal without a fight.
how: Oblique incision about two centimetres above and parallel to the medial two thirds of the inguinal ligament.
Divide skin, Camper and Scarpa fascia, controlling the superficial epigastric and external pudendal vessels.
Open the external oblique aponeurosis along its fibres from the superficial ring laterally, protecting the nerves lying immediately beneath it.
structuresAtRisk: Ilioinguinal nerve, directly under the external oblique aponeurosis
pitfalls: Cutting the ilioinguinal nerve while opening the aponeurosis.
An incision placed too low, over the ligament rather than above it.

step.hern.cord.title: Mobilising the cord and identifying the nerves
step.hern.cord.why: Every structure that causes a long-term complication is identified at this step: the vas, the vessels and the three nerves.
how: Mobilise the cord at the pubic tubercle where the plane is easiest, and encircle it with a sling.
Identify the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and make a deliberate decision to preserve each.
Palpate and inspect the cord for an indirect sac, and the floor for a direct defect. Then inspect the femoral canal.
pitfalls: Stripping the cord bare and devascularising the testis.
Failing to look for a second, femoral, hernia.

step.hern.sac.title: Dealing with the sac
step.hern.sac.why: How the sac is handled determines scrotal haematoma, testicular problems and, in the emergency setting, whether dead bowel is recognised.
how: Separate an indirect sac from the cord structures up to the deep ring, then transfix and excise it, or simply invert a small one.
Do not dissect a large scrotal sac out completely: divide it and leave the distal part open, which reduces haematoma.
Invaginate a direct sac rather than opening it.
In an incarcerated hernia, open the sac and hold the contents BEFORE releasing the constriction, so nothing non-viable escapes into the abdomen.
structuresAtRisk: Vas deferens adherent to the sac
pitfalls: Complete excision of a large scrotal sac, causing a substantial haematoma.
Releasing the neck of a strangulated sac before controlling the contents.

step.hern.mesh.title: Placing and fixing the mesh
step.hern.mesh.why: A tension-free mesh repair works because of overlap and a secure medial corner. Both recurrence and chronic pain are decided at this step.
how: Use a mesh large enough to overlap the pubic tubercle medially by about two centimetres and to extend well lateral to the deep ring.
Fix the medial corner securely onto the rectus sheath over the pubic tubercle, not into periosteum.
Suture the inferior edge to the shelving edge of the inguinal ligament; keep well away from the femoral vessels.
Create a slit around the cord and recreate a snug deep ring, then lay the mesh with a slight dome rather than stretched flat.
structuresAtRisk: Ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves caught in a fixation suture
pitfalls: A mesh that stops at the pubic tubercle rather than overlapping it.
A suture through periosteum, a recognised cause of persistent pain.
A slit made too tight or too loose around the cord.
